​The second post reads: "Do not underestimate the power of this technology. record.text: Most beginners feel frustrated with video editing not because they lack creativity, but because pro software throws them into dozens of tracks and parameters, they don't quite understand yet.

external.description:
Most beginners feel frustrated with video editing not because they lack creativity, but because pro software throws them into dozens of tracks and parameters, they don't quite understand yet. So, it's important to know where you are on the path from newcomer to veteran and find the right video editor to boost your confidence.

After trying them hands-on, I list 6 easy-to-pro video editing programs for Windows/Mac, and some for Linux and mobiles. Learn about their key features, modern AI strengths, and ease of use. You'll find one that suits you best.

## Top 6 Video Editing Software Compared

**Software** |  **Platforms** |  **Ease of Use** |  **Best For**
---|---|---|---
**CapCut** |  Windows, Mac, iOS, Android, Web |  Very Easy |  Social media beginners
**Tipard Video Converter Ultimate** |  Windows, Mac |  Very Easy |  Conversion plus light editing
**Kdenlive** |  Windows, Mac, Linux |  Easy |  Budget creators & new YouTubers
**Final Cut Pro** |  Mac, iPad |  Easy to Moderate |  Mac users
**Premiere Pro** |  Windows, Mac |  Moderate |  Pros & agencies
**DaVinci Resolve** |  Windows, Mac, Linux |  Advanced |  Filmmakers & colorists

## 1. CapCut

CapCut is probably the easiest editing software for starting off. It demands little from your hardware. Templates and auto features help you create fancy clips easily. What's better, it offers presets for vertical videos and direct sharing online, very sociable.

One possible disappointment is the paywalls. I used some features and templates, liked the effects, and then found the export option locked behind paywalls – it showed me the effects to encourage payment. But luckily, it's still among the best free video editing apps with most core editing features on the house.

**Platforms:** Windows, Mac, iOS, Android, and browser

**Free Limit:** Some templates, effects, and advanced AI tools require Pro.

**Pricing:** Pro from $19.99/month or $179.99/year

**Learning Curve:** Easiest

**Best for:** Beginners with average hardware, and short-form creators on TikTok, Reels, Shorts, etc.

## 2. Tipard Video Converter Ultimate

Tipard Video Converter Ultimate is also a simple video editing software for Windows/Mac. As a dedicated converter, it contains light but decent editing tools: trimming, cropping, rotation & flip, filters, visual effects, organized in a clear and pleasant interface. I picked it up in minutes even without a guide.

It stands out in its broad support of 500+ video and audio formats, up to 4K resolution. The resolution presets for specific social media and devices really make things easy.

**Platforms:** Windows, Mac

**Free Limit:** Up to 5-minute output.

**Pricing:** Lifetime $56 for 1 PC; monthly $18

**Learning Curve:** Very Easy

**Best for:** Users who need excellent format conversion and compression, along with light editing.

## 3. Kdenlive

Kdenlive feels like a natural next step once you've outgrown simple cutting. It offers a proper multi-track timeline, an effects collection, keyframe animation, color correction, and proxy editing that makes 4K manageable even on average hardware.

The UI looks a little cluttered and plain, and it doesn't have templates or AI-powered smart tools, so it takes a bit more to learn.

**Platforms:** Windows, Mac, Linux

**Free Limit:** Fully free with no limit

**Pricing:** Free and open-source

**Learning Curve:** Easy to Moderate

**Best for:** Casual creators and intermediate creators. Best video editing software for YouTube beginners.

## 4. Final Cut Pro

Final Cut Pro is a great video editing app for Mac users. It's developed by Apple itself and optimized for Apple Silicon. It uses a unique trackless magnetic timeline, meaning clips automatically snap together. You can move a clip around freely without asking "At what time should it come in?".

I can hardly say anything bad about it. The biggest limitation is probably the platform: it's Mac and iPad-only.

**Platforms:** Mac, iPad

**Free Limit:** 1-month free trial via Apple Creator Studio.

**Pricing:** $299.99 one-time for Final Cut Pro, or $12.99/month included in Apple Creator Studio

**Learning Curve:** Moderate

**Best for:** Mac users who want fast speed and professional experience.

## 5. Adobe Premiere Pro

Adobe Premiere Pro is the industry standard. It's built for serious long-form work. Advanced projects like multi-cam, color correction, audio mixing, and complex motion graphics are where it rules. It's also integrated with Adobe After Effects, Photoshop, and Audition, so you can transfer projects freely.

The trade-off is a steeper learning curve. It also demands decent hardware if you're working on high-res videos, like 4K.

**Platforms:** Windows, Mac, iPhone

**Free Limit:** 7-day full free trial.

**Pricing:** $22.99/month in the annual plan

**Learning Curve:** Moderate

**Best for:** Professionals, agencies, teams, and those already working in the Adobe ecosystem.

## 6. DaVinci Resolve

You've probably heard of DaVinci Resolve, one of the best free video editors. People speak highly of it because it provides pretty much anything a professional editor needs: video trimming, editing, AI enhancement, color grading with nodes and scopes, and even a complete audio toolbox. It has everything you need, and remains permanently free to access.

With all its strong features, it needs a high-end GPU and has a steep learning curve. It took me, an absolute beginner, about 4 hours to get the hang of the basics, and there's still a lot more to learn about.

**Platforms:** Windows, Mac, Linux

**Free Limit:** Permanent free version with core features. Advanced AI tools, noise reduction, and 4K+ resolutions require the paid Studio.

**Pricing:** $295 one-time for Studio

**Learning Curve:** Steep

**Best for:** Serious filmmakers on a budget. It's also the best free editing software for 4K videos.

## Final Recommendation

**Best for short vertical videos:** CapCut

**Best format compatibility:** Tipard Video Converter Ultimate

**Best free powerhouse:** DaVinci Resolve

**Best for pro users on Mac:** Final Cut Pro

**Industry standard:** Premiere Pro

## Conclusion

For those new to video production, CapCut and Tipard Video Converter Ultimate are the best video editing programs for beginners. When you grow into an advanced creator, Premiere and DaVinci Resolve will be your ultimate choices.

record.text: Nintendo showed Ocarina of Time in motion for the first time, dated a Zelda Switch 2 for October 29, and gave the movie a title but no trailer.

external.description:
Nintendo celebrated 40 years of The Legend of Zelda, and I have to admit, the anniversary Direct gave me quite a lot to take in.

Going into the showcase, I expected Nintendo to finally show more of the Ocarina of Time remake. What I didn't expect was just how much the company had prepared around it. We got our first proper gameplay look at the remake, a release date, new Zelda-themed hardware, collectibles, music announcements, an expanded Zelda Notes experience, and, finally, an official title and release date for the long-awaited live-action The Legend of Zelda movie.

But for me, there was one announcement that immediately stood above everything else: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being remade exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2.

After years of fans wondering what Nintendo might do with one of the most influential games in the history of the medium, seeing the remake in motion was easily the highlight of the entire presentation.

And what's particularly interesting is that Nintendo doesn't appear to be simply rebuilding Ocarina of Time with prettier graphics. The remake introduces new movement options, fully voiced characters, new progression tools, changes to familiar locations, and features designed specifically around the Switch 2.

At the same time, Nintendo seems very conscious of what made the original special.

The remake launches on November 5, 2026, and based on what Nintendo showed, I think there is going to be a lot to talk about between now and release.

Here's everything Nintendo announced during The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct.

10 Biggest Announcements from Nintendo Direct June 2026Nintendo’s June 2026 Direct delivered an Ocarina of Time remake, Kingdom Hearts IV, Xenoblade Genesis, and a clearer roadmap for Switch 2 through 2027.TechloyEmmanuel Umahi

## Ocarina of Time Remake Finally Gets Its First Gameplay Reveal

This was the moment I was waiting for.

Nintendo producer Eiji Aonuma took viewers through an extended gameplay demonstration of Ocarina of Time, giving us our first real idea of how Nintendo is approaching the remake.

The first thing that stood out to me was how familiar everything still feels.

The demonstration begins in Kokiri Forest, where Link meets Saria, but the entire environment has been rebuilt with modern visuals. Nintendo has also added new dialogue, giving characters more room to express themselves instead of simply reproducing the original game's conversations word for word.

Link himself feels considerably more modern.

He can now jump manually and swim, while movement options such as sprinting and rolling have been updated. That should make exploring Hyrule feel considerably less restrictive than it did in the original game.

Combat, thankfully, still looks recognizable. Link can use familiar weapons such as his sword and Deku Nuts, while the Fairy Slingshot returns with classic moments intact, including the puzzle where Link shoots an eye to lower a ladder.

I particularly like the fact that Nintendo isn't trying to erase every trace of the original game.

Even loading screens between certain areas remain. Aonuma explained that Nintendo deliberately kept them to preserve some of the feeling of playing the original Ocarina of Time.

That is a surprisingly important detail to me. A remake doesn't necessarily need to modernize everything just because it can.

## Threads of Time Gives Link's Journey a New Progression System

One of the more interesting additions is a feature called Threads of Time.

It tracks Link's progress through the adventure and displays his current objective, while a tapestry gradually fills in as players move through the story.

On paper, it sounds like a simple quality-of-life feature. But it could be particularly useful for players experiencing Ocarina of Time for the first time.

The original game was never exactly difficult to follow, but modern players are accustomed to having a clearer understanding of where they have been, what they have accomplished, and what they should be doing next.

Nintendo is also changing how some locations feel.

Hyrule Castle Town, for example, has been transformed from the original game's more restricted perspective into a third-person environment. Time will also continue moving while Link is inside towns, allowing players to actually watch the transition from day to night.

It's a small change, but it makes Hyrule feel more like a living world.

## You Can Hum Zelda Songs Into the Switch 2 Microphone

This might be one of the strangest additions, but I genuinely want to try it.

The Ocarina still works as expected, including its ability to manipulate the time of day, but Nintendo is now using the Switch 2's built-in microphone in an interesting way.

record.text: The companies with the strongest AI for ecommerce sellers may not be the ones with the flashiest models. They may be the ones quietly automating the work sellers spend hours doing every week, the work customers never see, but businesses can't operate without.

external.description:
The AI automation race in e-commerce has become predictable in some ways. Every week, there's another tool that promises to write better product descriptions, generate marketing images, or help sellers brainstorm keywords in seconds. Those capabilities are becoming table stakes. If one AI model can do it today, another will probably do it tomorrow.

But that's not where most online businesses lose time.

The harder part of e-commerce nowadays is beyond generating content. It's executing hundreds of small operational tasks across Amazon, Shopify, TikTok Shop, eBay, WooCommerce, and every other platform where a business sells. Updating listings. Monitoring competitors. Adjusting advertising campaigns. Keeping inventory and pricing in sync. The work is repetitive, messy, and spread across multiple systems.

That's creating a different kind of battle for ecommerce AI tools.

According to StoreClaw's internal usage data, sellers preparing for the second half of the year are spending less time using AI to write listings and more time connecting storefronts, analysing products, creating marketing assets, and managing advertising workflows. The shift doesn't necessarily describe the entire e-commerce industry, but it does suggest StoreClaw's users are looking for something different from AI automation: a tool that executes work instead of simply generating ideas.

And that's exactly where StoreClaw is trying to build its moat.

## **The data shows sellers are changing how they use AI**

Back-to-school season is often a preview of what happens before the Q4 shopping rush. Between late July and early August, StoreClaw saw a noticeable change in how its most active U.S. sellers used the platform.

The share of heavy users connecting live commerce platforms increased from 11.4% to 15.6%, while connected users grew by 19.6% during the same period. Image and video creation increased 4.5 percentage points, from 7.3% to 11.8%.

That is important because it suggests sellers have moved beyond experimenting with AI-generated text.

Instead, they're investing more in AI ecommerce operations that help prepare stores before holiday demand arrives.

As StoreClaw co-founder Steven Zhou puts it:

"Historically, enterprise retailers win Q3 and Q4 because they out-resource everyone else on speed and execution. A small seller can have a far superior product, but if they are manually updating inventory, tweaking prices product by product, or taking days to syndicate listings across platforms, they're too far behind. AI-driven operation is no longer optional; it is the key to achieving the speed required to stand out during peak surges."

## **The "dirty work" is where the moat lives**

Ask ChatGPT or Claude to help run an online store and you'll probably get product descriptions, email campaigns, SEO ideas, or social media captions.

Useful? Absolutely.

Enough to run a business? Not really.

StoreClaw's approach is built around the work that happens after those ideas are generated. Rather than acting as another writing assistant, it packages recurring ecommerce workflow automation into pre-built AI Skills that sellers can use without writing prompts from scratch.

That includes identifying products with genuine demand before stocking inventory, creating marketplace-ready listings that reflect customer pain points, monitoring competitor pricing and reviews, and analysing advertising campaigns to identify wasted spend.

The distinction sounds small, but it's an important product difference.

General-purpose AI generates outputs. StoreClaw is trying to automate decisions and workflows. That's the important difference between AI assistance and ecommerce AI automation.

That's a much harder product to build.

## **Why Amazon and Shopify probably won't solve this problem**

It's easy to assume Amazon or Shopify could build similar cross-platform ecommerce automation tools. They have the engineering talent, seller data, and AI infrastructure.

The bigger question is whether they have a reason to.

Amazon benefits when merchants become better Amazon sellers. Shopify benefits when businesses build deeper into Shopify's ecosystem. Helping sellers operate seamlessly across Amazon, Shopify, TikTok Shop, eBay, and WooCommerce doesn't strengthen those ecosystems; it weakens the incentive for merchants to stay inside one.

StoreClaw's value proposition is almost the opposite.

It connects natively with more than 20 commerce platforms and storefronts, creating a layer that sits between marketplaces instead of inside one of them.

That's a strategic difference, not just a feature.

## **The moat isn't the model**

AI models are improving quickly, and many of today's features will become widely available across different products.

StoreClaw's competitive argument is different.

Its moat isn't a proprietary language model or a smarter chatbot. It's the operational infrastructure built around e-commerce: cross-platform integrations, specialised workflows, marketplace-specific knowledge, and business data that gives AI enough context to execute real tasks.

That's a harder advantage to copy than another AI writing assistant.

As e-commerce becomes more fragmented across marketplaces, social commerce, and multiple storefronts, the value may increasingly come from the AI that quietly handles the messy operational work in the background, the work sellers rarely talk about but spend hours doing every week.

## **Why execution needs business context**

This is also where general-purpose AI starts to hit a wall.

A chatbot can recommend keywords or rewrite a listing, but it doesn't know which of your products are underperforming, how much you're spending on ads, which competitors are discounting products today, or whether inventory is running low.

StoreClaw's workflows are built around that context.

Its AI doesn't work from generic prompts alone. It works from store-level information, campaign history, competitor activity, pricing signals, and marketplace data. That gives it enough context to recommend actions that are tied to an actual business instead of hypothetical advice.

The AI isn't simply creating content. It creates recommendations based on live operational data.

## **The case studies say more than the feature list**

The strongest evidence for execution-focused AI isn't the number of features. It's whether those workflows change outcomes.

Take four StoreClaw customers.

INCENZO, a three-person Shopify fragrance business, reported 142% growth in organic traffic, while automating around 18 hours of SEO work every week and reducing customer acquisition costs by 57%. The takeaway isn't better at copywriting; it's less manual operational work.

Twinkle Star, an Amazon LED décor seller, cut product launch time from five to seven days down to 1.5 days while increasing conversion rates from 9.3% to 14.1%. That points to execution speed becoming a competitive advantage during busy sales periods.

Ruvalino saw repeat purchases increase from 11% to 18% alongside stronger organic search visibility. That's an example of AI supporting customer retention, not just customer acquisition.

LuxClub reduced the Advertising Cost of Sales from 35% to 22%, saved more than $80,000 per month in advertising spend, and reported a 47% quarter-over-quarter sales increase. Here, AI wasn't generating ads; it was helping improve campaign efficiency.

Each example reinforces the same point: execution-focused AI creates value by reducing operational friction.

## **The moat isn't the model**

Language models are improving quickly, and many AI features will eventually become widely available across competing products.

StoreClaw's competitive argument is different.

Its moat isn't a proprietary AI model or a smarter chatbot. It's the operational layer built around e-commerce: cross-platform integrations, specialised workflows, marketplace-specific knowledge, and business context that allows AI to execute real tasks.

That's significantly harder to replicate than another AI writing assistant.

As online retail becomes more fragmented across marketplaces, social commerce, and independent storefronts, the companies with the strongest AI for ecommerce sellers may not be the ones with the flashiest models. They may be the ones quietly automating the work sellers spend hours doing every week, the work customers never see, but businesses can't operate without.
